name: Client-Server Model
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Who's in Charge? The Client-Server Model and Its Tradeoffs
lesson.summary: Explains how most internet applications rely on clients requesting data from centrally controlled servers, and examines the convenience and the single-point-of-dependency risk that arrangement creates.
lesson.body:
Most of the internet applications people use every day, a banking app, a search engine, a streaming service, are built on the client-server model. In this arrangement, a client, typically the app or browser on your device, sends a request to a server, a more powerful computer or cluster of computers owned and operated by the company providing the service. The server processes the request and sends back a response. When you search for something online, your browser, the client, sends your query across the internet architecture described in the last chapter to a data center, the server, which looks up results and returns them.

This model has clear practical advantages. Centralizing data and processing on servers the provider controls makes it much easier to update software, since only the server side needs to change rather than every user's device. It makes it easier to enforce rules, moderate content, and maintain a single consistent version of information, since the server is the authoritative source of record. And it lets a service scale its infrastructure independently of how many or how few resources any individual user's device has.

But the model has a corresponding cost: whoever runs the server holds significant control and becomes a single point of dependency. If the server goes offline, due to a technical failure, a cyberattack, or a company decision, clients lose access, sometimes to data they consider their own. If the operator changes its policies, restricts access, or shuts down the service entirely, users generally have no independent way to keep using it, because the client software was never designed to function without that specific server. This maps directly onto the digital trust problem from earlier: using a client-server application generally means trusting one company's servers, and by extension the company itself, to behave honestly, stay operational, and protect your data.

A concrete example makes this tangible. Email built on open protocols can, in principle, be moved between providers, but a social media account, the posts, the follower connections, the messages, typically exists only on that platform's servers in a form the platform controls. If the company deletes your account, restricts it, or ceases to operate, that data and those connections are usually not recoverable elsewhere in the same form, because there was never a copy stored outside the company's servers.

None of this makes the client-server model a bad design; it is the right tradeoff for an enormous number of applications where having one clear, accountable party in charge is exactly what users want. But it is a specific choice, not the only way to structure a network, and the next chapter looks at the main alternative: a model where no single server holds that kind of authority at all.
